prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms to clocks at the 10^-18 level of uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep B013 as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye. After the full first-round exchange the scientific case has not weakened and the competition has narrowed to B013 and B001, which share no laureates. B013 rests on one identifiable idea and one identifiable realisation. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift on the clock transition, so that many neutral atoms can be held without Doppler or recoil shifts and interrogated together. Ye's group then showed what that ensemble could do, reaching systematic uncertainty and stability near 1e-18 and opening the many-body regime of the clock. Independent Sr and Yb clocks in several national laboratories confirm it, and the consequences are measured: intercontinental comparisons, centimetre-level relativistic geodesy, bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings, and the evidence base for redefining the second. As a theorist who has seen how much of the error budget (blackbody shifts, hyperpolarisability, lattice-induced shifts) depends on atomic-structure calculation, I am confident the physics is understood in detail and not merely impressive. My reasoning for putting it first is not that more members now name it, which I do not treat as evidence. It is that every Higgs trio proposed in round 1 differs from the others, and none of the supporters has offered a principle that selects three of four names. I regard the Higgs result as the larger scientific event and would not oppose it, but I judge the committee cannot defend a specific three-name allocation as well as it can defend Katori and Ye. My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1, but my reasons are now more explicitly comparative, and the main change in my thinking is that I accept a narrower framing of the citation, as set out below.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains overlap and scale. The 2005 prize honoured the optical frequency comb and the 2012 prize ion control, so a sceptic can read lattice clocks as a refinement of a well-served metrology lineage. Compared with the Higgs observation, the consequences for fundamental physics are narrower, and the practical culmination, the redefinition of the second, is still pending. There is also a real credit gap that two names do not close: Lemonde and the Paris group, Takamoto, the German groups (Lisdat, Sterr), the NIST and JILA team members and the ion-clock pioneers each made contributions that the citation can only acknowledge indirectly. If the committee judged that a defensible Higgs attribution exists, the Higgs would have a strong claim to outrank B013 on significance, and I would have to weigh that honestly.

responses.point: The Higgs discovery is the clearest uncredited experimental milestone, a trio balanced across ATLAS and CMS (Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee) covers the leadership, and the attribution problem is a reason to choose names carefully rather than to defer.
responses.response: Ulf's science is not in dispute from my side, and the chair's question is the right one: what principle selects the trio? Your own text says the choice is a judgement between leadership at the time of announcement and founding-era conception and that you rely on general knowledge of roles. Johansson's trio and yours differ on Virdee versus Della Negra, and the chair notes that Pearce moved too. A principle that gives one answer from the record has not appeared, and a prize that credits conception, construction and leadership for two collaborations of thousands will be read as a prize for four equally strong claims with one omitted. I would support Higgs if the Higgs supporters converge on a single trio with a stated rule, but I cannot treat that as settled today. I notice that you also list B013 as your first alternative, which means that on the question of defensibility we may be closer than the preferred configurations suggest.

responses.point: Attribution is a reason to choose names carefully and not to defer an overdue result, but B013 is a serious alternative and the redefinition of the second is still pending, so he would not rank it above the Higgs.
responses.response: Göran, I take your point that the Higgs discovery should not be deferred merely because attribution is hard, and I agree that the 2013 prize left the experimental half unrecognised. We differ on how to weigh that. The pending redefinition of the second does not, for me, reduce B013's maturity, because the 1e-18 performance has been reproduced independently and the redefinition is a metrological decision that follows the science rather than a test of it. On the other hand, your own uncertainty section concedes that your trio of Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni omits the CMS spokesperson at the time of the discovery, and Pearce and Danielsson draw the opposite conclusion. I would ask the Higgs side whether it can state a rule, for instance founders of the proposals versus the leaders who announced the result, and apply it identically to both experiments. If it can, I will reconsider; if not, B013 is the configuration I can defend name by name.

responses.point: The lattice clock is a distinct enabling idea and not a refinement of the comb, and the committee may wish to consider recusal on B013 because of Kroll's research stay in John Hall's laboratory, where Jun Ye is associated.
responses.response: I agree with Stefan on distinctness and I would add that the citation should say what is new, many neutral atoms held at the magic wavelength, so that it does not read as a general prize for precision clocks. On his disclosure, I think it is right that he raised it, but a stay in Hall's laboratory during doctoral work is a general connection to a group in which Ye was later a leading figure, not a documented collaboration with either credited name, and I do not believe it should force recusal. Eriksson and Mehlig have noted that B013 does not depend on Stefan's vote, and I would add that the question is not whether he is conflicted but whether the committee wishes to treat the disclosure as a recorded note. I would prefer the committee record the disclosure and let him vote, with the same standard applied to my own proximities.

responses.point: B046 should not narrow the credit by dropping Bistritzer, because Bistritzer and MacDonald wrote the decisive paper together, and the timing concern remains because the origin of the superconductivity is debated.
responses.response: Eva, you are right and I accept the correction. In round 1 I listed B046 as an alternative without being explicit about names, and the chair's summary records that I credit only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero. That was too narrow. The continuum-model prediction of the magic angle is a joint paper by Bistritzer and MacDonald, and if the committee ever takes up B046 the credited names should be MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero, with Cao's role in the experiments acknowledged in discussion. I still regard it as an alternative and not a preference for the reason you give: the field is about eight years old and the mechanism of the superconductivity is debated. I would not move it forward in this vote. Your point about attribution being settled from the record, not by dropping the least famous name, also applies equally to my own ballot, where I have to say why Katori and Ye and not Lemonde or Takamoto.

responses.point: A two-part prize pairing the Higgs with optical lattice clocks may be preferable to a single part, but the three-person cap makes it hard to credit fairly.
responses.response: Mark, I looked at this seriously because it would answer the question of significance against attribution. The numbers do not work. B013 has two names, so the whole configuration would leave one person for the Higgs, which would be arbitrary in the extreme, and a two-part prize in which one part is credited to a single leader of a collaboration of thousands is worse than either single part. The cap is therefore a scientific constraint here and not a technicality: a two-part prize is only workable if both parts have one or two clean names, and B001 does not. I would therefore keep the choice as B013 or B001 and not combine them. You also name B013 as your first alternative, which suggests you share the concern that a defensible Higgs trio is unproven.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes as disqualifying or as a natural continuation; my answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice solves a different problem, but others may disagree.

Whether the citation should name the neutral-atom lattice narrowly or precision optical clocks broadly; I prefer the narrow framing, with the 1e-18 realisation named, to keep credit with the people who made many-atom operation possible.
Whether the Higgs supporters can agree on a single trio with a stated principle, which is the one development that would change my preferred configuration.
Whether the redefinition of the second will take place before the decision. I do not think it changes the science, but it would strengthen the maturity argument if it did.

My recollection of exact priority dates and individual roles among Katori, Takamoto, Lemonde and the Boulder groups, and in the ATLAS and CMS leadership, is from general knowledge and is not verified from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B013 from my profile: I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye, although I work in precision atomic structure that is used across the clock community and have a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier on attosecond photoionisation, which is a separate field. For other ballots I continue to disclose my documented collaboration with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, where Andreas Wallraff (B054) is based, and my field's closeness to cold-atom lattice physics (B050). I would recuse myself from decisions on those ballots if the committee judged it a conflict, and none of them is in my preferred configuration. I note Kroll's disclosure on B013 and Johansson's on B054 as their own flags, not mine.
